input.title: Agent skill: document-modeling
input.author: skill-add
input.content:
---
name: document-modeling
description: Use when creating, extending, or redesigning a Powerhouse document model — defining or changing its state schema, modules, operations, operation errors, or reducer implementations.
---

# Document Modeling

Document models are defined through the reactor, never hand-written. Every file under `document-models/<model>/` —
`gen/`, `src/reducers/*.ts`, `schema.graphql`, tests — is generated by Vetra's watcher from the document-model
document. Never hand-write under `document-models/`, nor edit inside `gen/` — overwritten next pass. **Exception:**
hand-edit `src/reducers/<module>.ts` to fix/extend an existing operation ([reducer-patterns.md](references/reducer-patterns.md)) —
only the reducer body text survives a later `docs mutate`. **Tests aren't exempt:** a later `docs mutate`
regenerates `tests/<module>.test.ts` to scaffold, silently deleting hand-written ones — see DM.03.2 first.

**The single most important fact this skill teaches:** a `reducer` body only reaches generated code when supplied
**inline in the same `ADD_OPERATION` call that first introduces that operation name under a model id** — codegen
writes it verbatim into `src/reducers/<module>.ts`. Adding an operation bare, then setting its reducer via
`SET_OPERATION_REDUCER`, **silently no-ops**: the stored spec updates, the generated file never does, codegen
still reports success. Tracked per model id, surviving document deletion — a model id that's had a bare
`addOperation` is burned; rebuild under a new one. See [reducer-patterns.md](references/reducer-patterns.md) to
fix an already-scaffolded operation (hand-edit `src/`) and for deletion/cleanup hazards.

Every `switchboard` call needs an explicit `--profile <name>` bound to your local reactor. Creating that profile
is normally a one-time **user** setup step, not the agent's (`switchboard init` needs a TTY) — if none exists,
stop and ask, per [00-check-prerequisites.md](references/00-check-prerequisites.md) (also covering the unattended
exception and `--op`/field-name discovery — illustrative only). `docs mutate` needs both `--op` and
`--input`/`--input-file` or it hangs in an interactive editor; prefer `--input-file` to avoid shell-escaping.

## Workflow

1. [Prerequisites](references/00-check-prerequisites.md) — DM.00
2. [Write the description](references/01-write-description.md) — DM.01
3. [Define state and operations](references/02-state-and-operations.md) — DM.02
4. [Implement reducers](references/03-implement-reducers.md) — DM.03

See [graphql-schema.md](references/graphql-schema.md) for schema conventions, including a root-type rename hazard
that can break the GraphQL API, and [reducer-patterns.md](references/reducer-patterns.md) for purity rules, the
complete example, and recovering a burned model id.

`ADD_MODULE` → `ADD_OPERATION` → `ADD_OPERATION_ERROR` is a dependent chain: each needs a prior entity's id.
`switchboard docs apply` reverses operation order — never use it here; issue sequential `docs mutate` calls
instead. MCP's `addActions`, if available, batches the whole chain in one call (ids are client-generated UUIDs,
referenceable early), each `addOperation` still carrying its reducer inline. Expect transient `⚠️ Skipped code
generation … must have at least one operation defined` warnings, even a harsher Vite SSR parse-error banner
mid-batch — both normal.

## Common mistakes

- **Hand-writing `document-models/` files, or hand-deleting a generated folder to "clean up."** Unsafe —
  see reducer-patterns.md.
- **Splitting `addOperation` from its reducer** — the single most consequential mistake; see above.
- **Non-deterministic reducers**, or fallbacks like `action.input.id || crypto.randomUUID()`. Dynamic values
  always come from `action.input`.
- **`<Model>GlobalState` naming, or renaming a root type** once in use.
- **Setting the document ID manually** — `docs create` never accepts one.
- **Throwing generic `Error`** instead of named errors via `ADD_OPERATION_ERROR`.

# Reference: 00-check-prerequisites.md

# DM.00 Check the prerequisites for creating a document model

## DM.00.1 Ensure you have the required input and context

- Ensure you know at least the informal name of the new document model and who its users are.
- Ensure you know which Reactor Package project this document model will be in.
- Rephrase the request for clarity if needed.

### Expected Task Outcome
The required input and context are available and the agent is ready to perform the next task.

## DM.00.2 Confirm the reactor is running and reachable

- Verify a Reactor Package project is running, per the `reactor-project` skill — start it if it isn't.
- Confirm a local `switchboard` profile exists per the `reactor-project` skill's profile check. If none does, **stop** and give the user the exact profile stanza to add themselves — do not edit `~/.switchboard/profiles.toml` yourself, and do not attempt `switchboard init` non-interactively (it requires a TTY and has no flags). If there is no human available to confirm (an unattended run), follow the `reactor-project` skill's unattended-path exception instead — the only case where writing that stanza yourself is acceptable — and report exactly what you wrote.
- Run `switchboard ping --profile <local-profile>` and confirm it succeeds. Never run a bare `switchboard` command here or elsewhere: the CLI acts on its configured profile, and the default profile on this machine can point at a remote/cloud reactor rather than the local one you just started.
- Confirm the Vetra Drive is visible (`switchboard drives list --profile <local-profile>`), along with its accompanying Preview Drive.

### Discover the exact operation and field names before using any of them

Every camelCase `--op` name used elsewhere in this skill (`setStateSchema`, `addModule`, `addOperation`, ...) is an example for `powerhouse/document-model`, not a guarantee — confirm it against the running instance first:

1. `switchboard introspect --profile <local-profile>` — caches the schema; required before `models list`/`models get` work (a fresh profile errors with "No introspection cache found... Run switchboard introspect first" until you do this).
2. `switchboard models get powerhouse/document-model --profile <local-profile> --format json` — lists every operation with its exact camelCase name and input-type name.
3. `switchboard schema --profile <local-profile>` — dumps the full introspection JSON; `models get` alone only gives you the input type's *name*, not its fields. Find the `<Type>_<OperationName>Input` type in this dump to see the actual field names before calling `docs mutate`.

Input field names are **not** predictable from the operation name and are inconsistent across document types — e.g. `powerhouse/package`'s `setPackageAuthorName` takes a field called `name`, while `powerhouse/document-model`'s `setAuthorName` takes `authorName`. Always check the concrete input type via step 3 rather than guessing.

**The introspection cache goes stale as soon as a new document model registers, mid-session.** Introspection is not only a one-time prerequisite — it must be rerun any time a document model you're working with comes online *after* your last `switchboard introspect`. Symptom: `switchboard docs create --profile <local-profile> --type <new-model-id> ...` (or any other command scoped to that model) fails with `No namespace found for document type "<type>". Run switchboard introspect first`, even though introspection already succeeded once earlier in this same session, before that model existed. This does **not** mean the model failed to register — it means the cached schema predates it. Rerun `switchboard introspect --profile <local-profile>` (step 1 above) once the model's subgraph should exist, and the error resolves.

## DM.00.3 Review the existing package specs and implementation

- Review any existing specification documents in the Vetra Drive and consider how the new document model will fit in.
- Review the package implementation code in the project folder to get a good understanding of the existing functionality.
- Run the project unit tests (`pnpm test`) and confirm that they are passing.
- Ensure that there are no pending previous changes. Commit outstanding changes if needed.

## DM.00.4 Ensure the Reactor Package information is sufficiently updated

- Read the `powerhouse/package` document in the Vetra Drive and check if the information is complete.

  - If the document does not exist yet, create a new one for your package before proceeding with the creation
    of document models and other specification documents.

- Consider the potentially expanded package scope with the new document model that will be added. Consider
  what an improved name, description, category, publisher + url and keywords could be.

- Decide if it's worth updating the information.

  - If you created a new package document, update it with the information you came up with.

  - If the package document already existed, don't be too strict — you should not update the package
    information often. If the existing data still fits the purpose, leave it.

### Expected Task Outcome
The Reactor Package information is up-to-date and reflects the expanded scope.

## Expected Scenario Outcome

All prerequisites are in place for the agent to start writing the document model description.

# Reference: 01-write-description.md

# DM.01 Write the document model description

Use `switchboard docs` commands for this scenario: `docs create` and `docs get` as below, plus `docs mutate`
with the named operations called out in DM.01.3 and DM.01.4. Do not create or edit any files directly.

## DM.01.1 Ensure the document model specification document exists in Vetra Drive

- Check the Vetra Drive to confirm if a preliminary document model specification (formal type: `powerhouse/document-model`) already exists for the document model you want to create.

- If it already exists, note the document ID in the task outcome.

- If it does not exist already, create it first:
  ```bash
  switchboard docs create --profile <local-profile> --type powerhouse/document-model --name "<Model Name>" --drive <vetra-drive>
  ```
  - Remember: when creating any document in a drive, including this one, NEVER set the document ID manually — `docs create` always assigns it for you.
  - Make sure to set the name and add the document to the correct drive.
  - After adding it, confirm you see the document model: `switchboard docs get --profile <local-profile> <document-id>`.

## DM.01.2 Start by listing the users who will use the new document model

### Example

```
- Pizza Plaza restaurant owner
- Pizza Plaza customers
- Pizza Plaza kitchen chefs
```

## DM.01.3 Come up with a good, concise description

A good description includes its users, how they will use the document in a typical workflow, and it narrows
its scope as much as possible by describing what will not be included.

### Example

```
The Pizza Plaza order document will be used by the restaurant owner, their customers and the kitchen chefs.
The restaurant owner will prepare the document by defining the menu categories, options and prices in it.
The customer will then use this menu to add the pizzas, sides and drinks they want to order to their basket.
They will see the itemized prices and the total. Once the order is placed, a kitchen chef will check off the
items one by one as ready.

The order document does not support customization options for the items and it does not track the entire lifecycle
of payment, delivery, etc. It is meant to be a reliable reference for what the restaurant offers, what the customers
wants, and what the kitchen has prepared.
```

### Restrictions

- The description must not be longer than two or three paragraphs of text
- The scope of a document model should be "small" in the sense that the state of the documents it describes
  should not contain more than a couple of kilobytes of JSON on average.
- The document model should be "simple" in the sense that it should focus on a single purpose and its business
  logic should be precise and predictable: easy to implement and test.

### Write the description

Write it with `switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op setModelDescription --input '{"description": "<the description text>"}'`.

### Wrap-up

Run `switchboard docs get --profile <local-profile> <document-id>` and verify that the description was correctly
written to the document model specification.

## DM.01.4 Fill out the remaining header fields

**⚠️ Hazard: "document type" vs. "document ID" — do not conflate them.** These fields sound alike but are
unrelated:

- The **document ID** is the Vetra Drive item's own identity (a PHID). Per DM.01.1, `docs create` always assigns
  this one for you — **NEVER set it manually.**
- The **document type** (below) is a model-level field describing what kind of documents this model produces —
  e.g. `pizza-plaza/order`. It is written with the `setModelId` operation. Despite the operation's name
  (`setModelId`), it does **not** touch the document ID above; it sets the document *type* string.

### Document Type and Name

- The document type must be of the form `{organization}/{document-type-name}`
  - For example: `pizza-plaza/order`
  - Write it with `switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op setModelId --input '{"id": "<organization>/<document-type-name>"}'`

- Make sure that the name is set in a human-readable, capitalized form
  - For example: `Pizza Plaza Order`
  - Make sure all extra spacing is removed and each word is capitalized
  - The name must match `/[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9 ]*/`. This is critical for the state schema later,
    which uses this name to derive the root type name.
  - Write it with `switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op setModelName --input '{"name": "<Model Name>"}'`

### Document File Extension

- Reduce the document type to an abbreviation of 2 to 4 characters with a dot in front
- Avoid abbreviations with problematic connotations
- For example: `pizza-plaza/order` => `.ppo`
- For example: `software-engineering/xml` => `.sxml`, not `.sex`
- Write it with `switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op setModelExtension --input '{"extension": "<.ext>"}'`

### Author fields

- Fill out the author name with yours
  - Write it with `switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op setAuthorName --input '{"authorName": "<Your Name>"}'`

- Fill out the website URL with the stakeholder's if you know it, or the package publisher's URL.
  If both are unknown, use `https://powerhouse.inc` as a default.
  - Write it with `switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op setAuthorWebsite --input '{"authorWebsite": "<https://...>"}'`

### Wrap-up

Run `switchboard docs get --profile <local-profile> <document-id>` and verify that all details are correctly
written to the document model specification.

# Reference: 02-state-and-operations.md

# DM.02 Create the state schema and operations

Use `switchboard docs mutate` for this scenario. Do not create or edit any document content directly — the
`--input-file` files this scenario asks you to write (e.g. `<schema.json>`, `<initial-state.json>`) are scratch
files that carry `docs mutate` input, not the document itself. Recall the schema conventions in
[graphql-schema.md](graphql-schema.md) throughout.

## DM.02.1 Define the global state schema

### Reread the document description and come up with an extended version with more detail

- Take the scope restrictions into account but don't include them in the extended description
- Consider example data
- Describe in more detail what the users can do with the data
  - Consider creation, modification, sorting/moving and removal of data objects
  - Consider actions with more advanced business logic
  - Consider workflow status transitions
- Consider the relationship between the document you're creating and other document types
  - While documents must always be self-contained data structures, other documents can
    be referenced with a `PHID` and, typically, a number of cached properties.

### Example

If the original document description reads like this:

```
The Pizza Plaza order document will be used by the restaurant owner, their customers and the kitchen chefs.
The restaurant owner will prepare the document by defining the menu categories, options and prices in it.
The customer will then use this menu to add the pizzas, sides and drinks they want to order to their basket.
They will see the itemized prices and the total. Once the order is placed, a kitchen chef will check off the
items one by one as ready.

The order document does not support customization options for the items and it does not track the entire lifecycle
of payment, delivery, etc. It is meant to be a reliable reference for what the restaurant offers, what the customers
wants, and what the kitchen has prepared.
```

An extended version can be this:

```md
The Pizza Plaza order document will be used by the restaurant owner, their customers and the kitchen chefs.
The restaurant owner will prepare the document by defining the menu categories, options and prices in it.

Example categories are 'Small Pizzas', 'Medium Pizzas', 'Large Pizzas', 'Sides', and 'Drinks'. The restaurant
owner will define them simply with a label, and sort them in the right order. The category options are the actual
products such as 'Peperoni Pizza', which should have a name, picture URL, short description sentence, and a
unit price. The restaurant owner can create and edit the product details, and they can order the products within
the category, and they can delete products.

The customer will then use this menu to add the pizzas, sides and drinks they want to order to their basket. They can
update the amount and remove products from their basket. They cannot add the same product to their basket twice. They
cannot change the order of the products in their basket. The products will simply appear in the same order as in the menu.

Customers will see the itemized prices and the total price of each basket line item. The restaurant owner will set a
tax rate on each product category, which will also be applied. Overall we're keeping track of unit price excl. taxes,
unit price incl. taxes, subtotal excl. taxes and subtotal incl. taxes, basket total excl. taxes, basket tax total per
tax rate, and basket total incl. taxes.

Customers can clear their entire basket and start over. They can add additional notes to the order, which they can do
to communicate for example allergies or delivery instructions.

**Workflow**

The document workflow enforces menu creation first, which is then locked down. As a second phase the customer will fill
their basket and confirm. Once confirmed, the basket can no longer be edited and the kitchen chef will check off the items.
Once all items are checked off, the order document is fulfilled. It is possible to go back to menu editing but then the
basket will be automatically cleared. There should be timestamps for each one of the status transitions.

**External documents**

The shop owner will reference a `pizza-plaza/point-of-sale` document in the `pizza-plaza/order` document, from where the
local name, company ID, address and telephone number will be cached.
```

### Extract an initial state schema from the extended description

**State Schema Root Type on line 1**

- **CRITICAL**: on the very first line of the state schema, there is always a single root type — see
  [graphql-schema.md](graphql-schema.md#state-type-naming) for the exact naming rule. Failing to apply it will
  break the code generator later on.

  For example: if the document model name is `Pizza Plaza Order`, its root type name is `PizzaPlazaOrderState`.

- The root type must not have an ID field (`OID` or `PHID`), because the document header already contains an
  ID. However, it may contain a business logic code or reference that the user would use as document identifier.

  For example: Pizza Plaza needs an _order id_ for their accounting. This should be a `String` field or another
  appropriate scalar type, but not an `OID` or `PHID` — for example `orderRef: String`.

**OIDs and PHIDs**

- All objects in collections (arrays) MUST HAVE an `id: OID!`. `OID` fields are used both as "primary key" and
  "foreign key reference". Good practice is to call the property `id` if it's a primary key, and call it
  `otherObjectId: OID!` if it's a foreign key, with a comment to define which object types it can reference.

- Use the `PHID` only to reference external documents if needed and identify the cached data properties
  that are needed.

  "Cached data property" simply means that a number of properties will be set together with the
  external document id so that the user can understand what was in the external document at the time when
  the PHID field was set. These data properties can get out-of-date, so the system will need to ensure it's
  updated when it matters — the same principle as the title and snippet information in an HTML link preview
  or social media card, where the cached description can go stale.

  Only use PHID fields when it's needed for the use case. Linking multiple documents always increases complexity.

- **NEVER** use the `ID` type. Instead use `OID` and `PHID` (see [graphql-schema.md](graphql-schema.md#scalar-types)).

- Always use `enum` types for workflow statuses.

**When to use mandatory and optional state fields**

Mandatory properties in a state and operation input schema are indicated with an exclamation mark, e.g. `id: OID!`.
Note that the reasoning about when to use mandatory fields in the state schema is quite different from the reasoning
about operation input schemas — we're only concerned with the former here.

- **IMPORTANT**: a user must always be able to create an empty document _without_ providing any information, and the
  state schema needs to cover the entire life cycle of the document. This means that, in the root type, _properties
  can only be mandatory if they have a logical default value_.

  For example, one might think: "A Pizza Plaza order always needs an order ID for their accounting, make it mandatory",
  but this overlooks the fact that the restaurant owner must be able to create an empty order document in the first place.
  Order ID in this case also does not have a logical default, because it has to be unique in the system. Therefore,
  the `orderRef: String` field should definitely not be mandatory.

- Collections, i.e. array types, should always use double exclamation marks like `lines: [BasketLine!]!`. The inner
  exclamation mark simply expresses that array items should never be a NULL value, which is always the case. The outer
  exclamation mark indicates that at least an empty array should always be set as value of the collection, as opposed to
  `lines = null`. Following our rule, this is almost always a very logical default.

- Another situation with a common 'logical default' is a child object. In our Pizza Plaza order example, the `menu: Menu!`
  should always _exist_, although it should be empty in the beginning. Note that this can only be done if the child object
  also has a logical empty default — mandatory properties of the child object may prevent this.

  The customer basket, however, may logically only come into existence when the document moves on to the "BASKET_EDITING"
  phase. Therefore it could be made optional as a design decision to reflect the lifecycle business logic: `basket: Basket`.

**Images and attachments**

There is no support for embedded images or attachments at the moment. Use the `URL` type to link images and attachments
in the document model.

**Collection sorting**

- There is no need to use a `position` or `weight` property to sort items in a collection. The items must be kept ordered
  in the array via their index.

- Since all collection objects have an `id: OID!`, moving and sorting operations can be defined as
  `SORT(ids: [OID!]!, insertBefore: OID)`. `insertBefore` is optional, not mandatory: omitting it (`null`) means
  "append at the end" — see `REORDER_CATEGORIES`/`REORDER_MENU_ITEMS` below for the pattern in practice. This is
  a best practice that creates operations that have good branching and merging behavior too.

**Trees and Recursion**

- Always define trees as a flat list, e.g. `TreeNodeType { id: OID!, parentId: OID }`, whereby root nodes have `parentId=null`.

- During reducer implementation, it's good practice to have a sorting helper function that deterministically sorts the tree
  nodes, e.g. depth-first, and apply this helper function in every reducer that manipulates the tree structure.

### Example

The initial state schema could be like this:

```graphql
type PizzaPlazaOrderState {
  status: OrderStatus!          # default = MENU_EDITING
  pos: PointOfSaleInfo          # mandatory child properties make this optional
  menu: Menu!                   # default = empty menu
  basket: Basket                # does not exist until status = BASKET_EDITING
  customerNotes: String         # optional
  timestamps: OrderTimestamps!  # default = empty timestamps
}

enum OrderStatus {
  MENU_EDITING
  BASKET_EDITING
  BASKET_CONFIRMED
  ORDER_FULFILLED
}

type PointOfSaleInfo {
  docId: PHID!                  # references pizza-plaza/point-of-sale document
  name: String!                 # cached property
  companyID: String!            # cached property
  address: String               # cached property
  telephone: String             # cached property
}

type OrderTimestamps {
  menuCreatedAt: DateTime
  basketConfirmedAt: DateTime
  orderFulfilledAt: DateTime
}

type Menu {
  categories: [MenuCategory!]!
}

type MenuCategory {
  id: OID!
  label: String!
  taxRate: Float!
  items: [MenuItem!]!
}

type MenuItem {
  id: OID!
  status: MenuItemStatus!
  name: String!
  picture: URL
  description: String
  unitPriceInclTax: Float!
}

enum MenuItemStatus {
  DRAFT,
  AVAILABLE,
  OUT_OF_STOCK
}

type Basket {
  lines: [BasketLine!]!
  totals: BasketTotals!
}

type BasketLine {
  id: OID!                  # Primary Key
  itemId: OID!              # Foreign Key: MenuItem.id
  quantity: Int!
  unitPriceExclTax: Float!
  unitPriceInclTax: Float!
  subtotalExclTax: Float!
  subtotalInclTax: Float!
  categoryTaxRate: Float!
  preparedByKitchen: Boolean!
}

type BasketTotals {
  totalExclTax: Float!
  taxBreakdown: [TaxRateTotal!]!
  totalInclTax: Float!
}

type TaxRateTotal {
  taxRate: Float!
  taxAmount: Float!
}
```

### Wrap-up

- Set the state schema via `switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op setStateSchema --input-file <schema.json>` for the `global` scope.
- Verify with `switchboard docs get --profile <local-profile> <document-id>`.

### Expected Outcome

The state schema of the document model is created following best-practice rules and written to the spec.

## DM.02.2 Generate a minimal default value for the document

Create a JSON object that complies to the root object type with only the mandatory properties filled.

### Example

Our empty `pizza-plaza/order` document would look as follows:

```json
{
  "status": "MENU_EDITING",
  "pos": null,
  "menu": {
    "categories": []
  },
  "basket": null,
  "customerNotes": null,
  "timestamps": {
    "menuCreatedAt": null,
    "basketConfirmedAt": null,
    "orderFulfilledAt": null
  }
}
```

### Wrap-up

- **The `setInitialState` operation input is `{scope, initialValue}`, not the raw state object itself** — `scope`
  is the plain string `"global"` (or `"local"`), and `initialValue` must be the state JSON **stringified into a
  single string**, not a nested JSON object. Build the `--input-file` around that shape, for example:
  ```json
  {
    "scope": "global",
    "initialValue": "{\"status\":\"MENU_EDITING\",\"pos\":null,\"menu\":{\"categories\":[]},\"basket\":null,\"customerNotes\":null,\"timestamps\":{\"menuCreatedAt\":null,\"basketConfirmedAt\":null,\"orderFulfilledAt\":null}}"
  }
  ```
  Passing the pretty-printed state object above directly as the `--input-file` content fails validation.
- Set the default value via `switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op setInitialState --input-file <initial-state.json>`.
- Verify with `switchboard docs get --profile <local-profile> <document-id>`.

### Expected Outcome

The default value JSON is available in the document and complies to the state schema.

## DM.02.3 Define the modules and operations titles

Keep the users of the new document model in mind and generate a list of operations grouped in modules.

### Example
```
Module 'menu_categories'
- ADD_CATEGORY(id:OID!, label:String!, taxRate:Float!)
- SET_CATEGORY_LABEL(id:OID!, label:String!)
- SET_CATEGORY_TAX_RATE(id:OID!, taxRate:Float!)
- REMOVE_CATEGORY(id:OID!)
- REORDER_CATEGORIES(orderedCategories:[OID!]!, insertBefore:OID)

Module 'menu_items'
- ADD_MENU_ITEM(categoryId:OID!, item:NewMenuItemInput!, insertBefore:OID)
- UPDATE_MENU_ITEM(id:OID!, item:MenuItemUpdateInput!)
- UPDATE_MENU_ITEM_STATUS(id:OID!, status:MenuItemStatus!)
- REMOVE_MENU_ITEM(id:OID!)
- REORDER_MENU_ITEMS(orderedMenuItems:[OID!]!, insertBefore:OID)

Module 'point_of_sale'
- SET_POINT_OF_SALE(docId:PHID!, name:String!, companyID:String!, address:String, telephone:String)
- UPDATE_POINT_OF_SALE_INFO(name:String, companyID:String, address:String, telephone:String)
- CLEAR_POINT_OF_SALE()

Module 'basket'
- ADD_LINE(id:OID!, menuItemId:OID!, quantity:Int)
- UPDATE_LINE_QTY(id:OID!, quantity:Int)
- REMOVE_LINE(id:OID!)

Module 'kitchen'
- MARK_ITEM_PREPARED(id:OID!)
- MARK_ITEM_TODO(id:OID!)

Module 'workflow'
- FINISH_MENU_EDITING(time:DateTime!)
- REOPEN_MENU_EDITING(time:DateTime!)
- CONFIRM_BASKET(time:DateTime!)
- MARK_ORDER_FULFILLED(time:DateTime!)
```

### Check consistency and correctness

- Remember that operation reducers are pure, deterministic functions
  - So we need to pass all OID values for new objects, for example: `ADD_CATEGORY` needs an `id:OID!` as input
  - And we need to pass all system-dependent data as input to avoid side effects, for example: `FINISH_MENU_EDITING` needs the `time`
- Users will have permissions on an operation level, so operations' responsibilities must be separated
  - For example: `MARK_ITEM_PREPARED` must be separated from `UPDATE_LINE_*`
- All state variables must be directly or indirectly controlled by the user
  - For example: `SET_CATEGORY_LABEL` is a straight-forward direct update
  - For example: `ADD_LINE`, `SET_CATEGORY_TAX_RATE`, ... sets the tax values/totals indirectly
  - For example: the workflow operations control the `status` field

### Submitting the dependent chain: sequential `docs mutate`, not `docs apply`

`ADD_MODULE` → `ADD_OPERATION` → `ADD_OPERATION_ERROR` is a dependent chain: each action needs the id of an
entity created by a prior one (an operation needs its module's id; an operation error needs its operation's id).

`switchboard docs apply` reverses operation order, so **never use `docs apply` for this chain**. Issue sequential
`docs mutate` calls instead — one action at a time, each with `--op` (camelCase: `addModule`, `addOperation`,
`addOperationError`) and `--input-file`:

```bash
switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op addModule --input-file module.json
switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op addOperation --input-file operation.json
switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op addOperationError --input-file error.json
```

**`addModule` is safe to call as soon as a module is planned.** `addOperation` is not: it is the one-time event
that scaffolds an operation's generated handler function, and per [reducer-patterns.md](reducer-patterns.md#the-reducer-field-is-the-code-inline-only)
the reducer can only ever be supplied in *that same call*. If you're not ready with the operation's complete
input schema and reducer body yet, don't call `addOperation` for it — plan its name and description here, but
defer the actual call to DM.03, once you're ready to submit schema and reducer together in one shot.

If the reactor's MCP tools are enabled instead (see the `reactor-project` skill), its `addActions` tool can submit
the *entire* chain — every module, operation (schema and reducer inline, per the same rule above), and error — in
**one** batched call. Module, operation, and error ids are client-generated UUIDs, so you can pre-generate all of
them and reference an id in an earlier action before the entity it names exists, as long as the array stays in
forward dependency order (modules, then their operations, then those operations' errors).

Expect transient warnings like `⚠️ Skipped code generation ... Module "basket" must have at least one operation
defined` while the batch is still landing — a normal intermediate state as modules and operations apply in
sequence, not a failure. A harsher-looking variant can also appear mid-batch: a hard Vite SSR `PARSE_ERROR`
(`Transform failed with 1 error... Unexpected token`, pointing at a generated `creators.ts`), from codegen having
written a partially-valid file before every operation in a module existed yet. It looks like a real crash — a
hard `ERROR` banner, not a soft `⚠️` warning — but it is the same kind of transient mid-batch inconsistency and
self-heals a few mutations later once the module is complete. Neither warning form means the batch failed; both
resolve once the whole batch has been applied and codegen re-validates against the final state.

- Create all modules (with name and description) in the document's `global` scope now; hold operations for DM.03 unless their schema and reducer are already finalized.

### Wrap-up

Verify the modules with `switchboard docs get --profile <local-profile> <document-id>`. Keep the planned
operation list (names, descriptions, module assignment) for DM.02.4 and DM.03 — it is not submitted yet.

### Expected Outcome

- All modules are now listed in the document model spec in Vetra Drive.
- Operations are planned (grouped by module) but not yet created — their input types and reducers still need
  to be worked out (DM.02.4) and submitted together (DM.03).

## DM.02.4 Define the operation inputs

Work out the input type text for every planned operation now, but do not submit operations yet — see DM.02.3:
`addOperation` is deferred to DM.03, where schema and reducer are submitted together in one call per operation.
See [graphql-schema.md](graphql-schema.md#input-type-conventions) for the input root type name rule, the
type-reference rules, and the empty-input-type work-around — they apply to every operation you design here.

### Knowing when to use mandatory / optional input type properties

Input types are about _user intent and the mutation that will be applied_. As such, properties in input types should
often be mandatory or optional even when they are (not) optional in the state schema. Optional input properties that are
set to null are either interpreted as "not included in the input" (add/patch-like operation) or could mean "clear this
value in the state."

- Due to this ambiguity, and because clearing data often should have a separate permission associated, it's often
  advisable to create a separate `CLEAR_PROPERTY` operation instead.

- For example: the `pizza-plaza/order` state schema has an optional `orderRef: String` state property because the order
  reference won't be set when the empty document is first created.

  - However, the `SET_ORDER_REF` operation's input type requires an `orderRef` parameter because, once set, the orderRef
    should generally not be cleared.

  - Should the requirement come up that an order ref, in fact, should be cleared in some cases, an additional
    `CLEAR_ORDER_REF` operation should be added.

### Wrap-up

- You should now have, for every planned operation: its module, name, description, and finished input schema
  text — everything `addOperation` needs except the reducer body.
- Nothing is submitted to the reactor yet for these operations. Proceed to DM.03, where each operation's
  reducer is written and the whole operation (schema + reducer) is submitted in a single `addOperation` call.

### Expected Outcome

- All modules exist in the document model spec in Vetra Drive.
- Every operation's schema is designed and ready, but not yet submitted — codegen has not scaffolded these
  operations' handler functions, so their reducers can still be supplied inline when they are.

# DM.03 Implement document model reducers

Work in the active Reactor Package project directory (see the `reactor-project` skill for starting/restarting it
and inspecting its logs). Read the project's `AGENTS.md` for local conventions.

Reducer implementation follows [reducer-patterns.md](reducer-patterns.md) — purity rules, the forbidden-function
list, the complete add/update/delete example, `Maybe`/`InputMaybe` handling, error conventions, and — critically —
the rule that a reducer only ever lands in generated code when supplied inline in the operation's first
`addOperation` call. This scenario does not restate that material, but its sequencing below depends on it.

Code is regenerated automatically by Vetra's watcher. If the code generator is stuck on a genuine error, review
the GraphQL types for mistakes and fix the document model specification via `switchboard docs mutate`. Do not
reach for restarting the reactor project as a first response — see [reducer-patterns.md](reducer-patterns.md#deletion-and-cleanup-are-not-safe-recovery-tools)
for what's actually recoverable without one, and [graphql-schema.md](graphql-schema.md#state-type-naming) for the
one hazard (a root-type rename) that does require a restart with no CLI-level alternative.

## DM.03.1 Confirm that the reducers boilerplate has been generated by Vetra

- Read the document model specification for context: `switchboard docs get --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --state`.
- In `document-models/<model>/v1/`, `gen/schema/types.ts` and `gen/schema/zod.ts` already exist from the state
  schema you submitted in DM.02.1 — read them for the exact TypeScript types of every scalar (especially
  `Amount_Money` → `number`, `Date` → `string`), confirming or replacing what you assumed from
  [graphql-schema.md](graphql-schema.md#graphql--typescript-mapping).
- No operation has been added yet if you followed DM.02.3/DM.02.4's deferral, so `gen/<module>/operations.ts`
  and `src/reducers/<module>.ts` won't exist for a brand-new model — that's expected, not a problem. If you're
  extending an existing model instead, read the already-generated `gen/<module>/operations.ts` and
  `src/reducers/<module>.ts` for the operations that already exist, and identify which of those need a fix
  (via hand-editing `src/`, per [reducer-patterns.md](reducer-patterns.md#the-reducer-field-is-the-code-inline-only) —
  `setOperationReducer` alone will not change them).
- Run `pnpm test` (this runs vitest) to know which tests are currently failing.
- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` to detect type errors (`pnpm tsc` maps to bare `tsc`, which emits files instead of just checking).

## DM.03.2 Implement and test the reducers one module at a time

Consider which order you will implement the operation modules in:
- Try to focus on the most complex modules first and verify the reducers' behavior.
- Save simple data setters until last unless they are a dependency.

For each **new** operation (the common case, per DM.02.3/DM.02.4's deferral), the process is one atomic step, not
two:

1. Write its complete, pure reducer body (per [reducer-patterns.md](reducer-patterns.md)), using the input
   schema you designed in DM.02.4.
2. Submit the **entire operation in one `addOperation` call** — module id, name, description, input schema, and
   the reducer body, all in the same `--input-file` payload:
   ```bash
   switchboard docs mutate --profile <local-profile> <document-id> --op addOperation --input-file operation.json
   ```
   Never call `addOperation` without its reducer, intending to add the reducer with a later `setOperationReducer`
   call — see [reducer-patterns.md](reducer-patterns.md#the-reducer-field-is-the-code-inline-only)
   for why that silently fails to reach the generated file.
3. Confirm `src/reducers/<module>.ts` now contains that reducer body verbatim, and that it compiles.

For an operation that **already exists** (you're fixing a bug found by tests, or extending prior work): hand-edit
`src/reducers/<module>.ts` directly. That edit is durable **only if no further `docs mutate` touches this document
afterward** — a subsequent mutation against the same document, including the `setOperationReducer` resync below,
regenerates the file from the stored spec and keeps only the reducer **body** text, silently clobbering everything
else you touched (parameter names, imports, comments). See
[reducer-patterns.md](reducer-patterns.md#the-reducer-field-is-the-code-inline-only) for the full mechanics. Also
resubmit `setOperationReducer` with the same body so the document model's *stored specification* stays in sync for
the future — but do this resync **last**, after every other hand-edit to this file in this pass, since the resync
call itself will re-clobber any non-body change made before it. Verify the fix by reading
`src/reducers/<module>.ts` itself, not by reading `docs get --state` back — the latter will show your new text even
on a submission that never reached the generated file.

**IMPORTANT**: keep the reducers and their parameters strictly typed. No `any` types are acceptable in the reducers
or their parameters, ever — their business logic needs to be strict and well-tested, and so should their type
structure be.

**IMPORTANT**: write a unit test for each reducer that does not use mock objects, and have the test check the
expected document state after applying the operation(s), to verify the business logic.

**CRITICAL — these hand-written tests are not durable across further mutations of this document.** Any later
`docs mutate` call against this same document — including the `setOperationReducer` resync above, or any further
`addOperation`/`addModule`/etc. on it — triggers a codegen pass that regenerates `tests/<module>.test.ts` back to
its auto-generated scaffold, **silently discarding every hand-written test you added**. There is no error and no
warning: the test count just shrinks, and `pnpm test` reports the smaller number as if nothing were missing. To
avoid losing this work:
- Finish **all** `docs mutate` calls against this document (including reducer resyncs) before you write or rely on
  hand-written tests for it, or
- Keep hand-written assertions in a file codegen does not own (e.g. `tests/<module>.behavior.test.ts` alongside the
  generated `tests/<module>.test.ts`), so they survive regardless of mutation order.
If you must interleave — write a test, hit a lint/type issue, resubmit a mutation to fix it — recheck your test
count with `pnpm test` after every `docs mutate` call, not only at the end, and re-add anything that vanished.

Rerun `pnpm test`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, and `pnpm lint:fix` (which runs oxlint — `oxlint --type-aware --type-check
--fix` — not ESLint, despite the name) until all issues are resolved before moving to the next module.

If you ever did add a bare operation (no reducer) under this model id — in this session or an earlier one — and
hand-editing `src/` isn't resolving it, treat the model id as burned; see
[reducer-patterns.md](reducer-patterns.md#the-reducer-field-is-the-code-inline-only) for
the recovery (a new model id, never `docs delete` followed by reusing the same one).

Do not proceed to the next reducers module until the last one is fixed.

## DM.03.3 Verify tests and type-check pass

- Verify that tests are passing via `pnpm test`.
- Verify that no type errors remain via `npx tsc --noEmit`.

# Reference: graphql-schema.md

# GraphQL Schema Conventions

Conventions for document model state schemas and operation input schemas. Referenced from [02-state-and-operations.md](02-state-and-operations.md) and [03-implement-reducers.md](03-implement-reducers.md).

## State type naming

The global state root type must be named `<DocumentModelName>State` — the PascalCase document model name plus `State`. Nothing else.

❌ Wrong:
```graphql
type TodoListGlobalState {
  todos: [Todo!]!
}
```

✅ Correct:
```graphql
type TodoListState {
  todos: [Todo!]!
}
```

Local scope (if used) follows the same rule with `LocalState`: `TodoListLocalState`.

**Why it matters:** the code generator expects exactly this type name to derive the root state type. A `GlobalState` suffix (or any other) compiles as valid GraphQL but breaks TypeScript codegen. Separately, Switchboard's stitched supergraph namespaces every model's types with `<ModelName>_` in introspection output (e.g. `PizzaOrderState` becomes `PizzaOrder_PizzaOrderState`) — that prefix is the supergraph's doing, not a sign your authored name is wrong.

**⚠️ Hazard: renaming the root type after the fact.** Get this name right on the model's very first `setStateSchema` call. Submitting a second `setStateSchema` that renames the root type on a document that's already had at least one successful codegen pass can permanently break the composed Apollo Gateway supergraph — not just for the renamed model, but for **every** model in the drive: every subgraph gets excluded from composition (`Excluding subgraph ... Unknown type <New>_<New>State`, then `No queries found in any subgraph`), and `http://localhost:<port>/graphql` stops answering any query, for any model, for the rest of the reactor process's life. `switchboard docs get`/`docs mutate` keep working throughout (they route around the composed gateway through the reactor's own storage), so you can still inspect and build via the CLI, but there is **no CLI-level recovery** for the broken composed schema — deleting the offending document does not fix it. The reactor process must be restarted to recompose the supergraph from scratch.

## Scalar types

| Standard  | Identity                        | Amount               | Specialized        |
| --------- | -------------------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------- |
| `String`  | `OID` (object id)                | `Amount`              | `EthereumAddress`   |
| `Int`     | `PHID` (Powerhouse document id)  | `Amount_Tokens`       | `EmailAddress`      |
| `Float`   | `OLabel`                          | `Amount_Money`        | `Date`              |
| `Boolean` |                                   | `Amount_Fiat`         | `DateTime`          |
|           |                                   | `Amount_Currency`     | `URL`               |
|           |                                   | `Amount_Crypto`       | `Currency`          |
|           |                                   | `Amount_Percentage`   |                     |

Never use the plain `ID` type — use `OID` or `PHID` instead.

## GraphQL → TypeScript mapping

| GraphQL scalar        | TypeScript type | Example value                  |
| ---------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `Amount_Money`         | `number`         | `99.99`                         |
| `Amount_Percentage`    | `number`         | `10.5`                          |
| `Amount_Fiat`          | `{ unit: string; value: number }` | `{ unit: "USD", value: 1000 }` |
| `Amount_Tokens`        | `number`         | `500`                           |
| `OID`                  | `string`         | `"item-001"`                    |
| `PHID`                 | `string`         | `"phd:..."`                     |
| `Date`                 | `string`         | `"2025-01-15"`                  |
| `DateTime`             | `string`         | `"2025-01-15T10:30:00.000Z"`    |
| `URL`                  | `string`         | `"https://example.com"`         |
| `EmailAddress`         | `string`         | `"user@example.com"`            |
| `EthereumAddress`      | `string`         | `"0x..."`                       |

Don't guess a scalar mapping — if unsure, read the generated `gen/schema/types.ts`, which contains the definitive `Scalars` map.

## Arrays and objects

- Arrays are always mandatory-of-mandatory: `[MenuItem!]!`, never `[MenuItem!]` or `[MenuItem]!`.
- Every object type that appears inside an array must carry `id: OID!` for identification.
- Add `OLabel` fields for display metadata where relevant.

## Input type conventions

Input types describe user intent for a mutation, not stored state — reason about mandatory/optional independently of the state schema's own rules.

### CRITICAL: Input root type name

The input root type must be named `<OperationName>Input`, the PascalCase of the operation name. For example, `SET_CATEGORY_LABEL` → `SetCategoryLabelInput`. Getting this wrong breaks compilation later.

### CRITICAL: Type references

- Only `enum` types (and scalars) from the state schema may be referenced directly inside an input type. Every other state object type needs its own mirror input type — never reference a state object type or reuse another operation's input type as-is.
- Never redefine a state enum inside an input type; reference it directly.

Example — given this state:
```graphql
type MenuItem {
  id: OID!
  status: MenuItemStatus!
  name: String!
  picture: URL
}

enum MenuItemStatus {
  DRAFT
  AVAILABLE
  OUT_OF_STOCK
}
```

Operations `ADD_CATEGORY_MENU_ITEMS` and `UPDATE_CATEGORY_MENU_ITEMS` need their own mirror input types, not `MenuItem` itself:
```graphql
"Operation: ADD_CATEGORY_MENU_ITEMS"
input AddCategoryMenuItemsInput {
  categoryId: OID!
  items: [NewMenuItemInput!]!   # mirrors MenuItem, does not reference it
}

input NewMenuItemInput {
  id: OID!                      # new item's OID, always required to keep reducers pure
  status: MenuItemStatus        # enum state type IS reusable directly — default = AVAILABLE
  name: String!
  picture: URL
}

"Operation: UPDATE_CATEGORY_MENU_ITEMS"
input UpdateCategoryMenuItemsInput {
  categoryId: OID!
  items: [MenuItemUpdateInput!]!  # a distinct mirror type, not NewMenuItemInput
}

input MenuItemUpdateInput {
  id: OID!
  status: MenuItemStatus        # default = no update
  name: String                  # default = no update
  picture: URL                  # default = no update
}
```

### CRITICAL: Empty input type work-around

An input type with zero fields isn't supported by the code generator:

❌ Fails:
```graphql
input ClearDescriptionInput {
}
```

✅ Add a dummy optional field as a work-around:
```graphql
input ClearDescriptionInput {
  _: Boolean
}
```

# Reference: reducer-patterns.md

# Reducer Patterns

Referenced from [03-implement-reducers.md](03-implement-reducers.md).

## The reducer field IS the code: inline only

The `reducer` string is written **verbatim** — reformatted by prettier, nothing else changed — into the body of an operation's handler function in `src/reducers/<module>.ts`, but **only when it is supplied inline in the same `ADD_OPERATION` call that first introduces that operation name under this model id.** That is the one and only moment codegen writes real reducer content into the generated file. Never call `addOperation` bare (name/schema, no reducer) intending to fill in the reducer afterward — always compose the complete operation, schema and reducer together, before submitting it.

**`SET_OPERATION_REDUCER` on an operation that already exists is a silent no-op on the generated file.** It updates the document model's *stored specification* — `docs get --state` will show your new text — but `src/reducers/<module>.ts` keeps whatever body it already had, with no error and no warning; codegen still reports `✅ Code generation completed successfully`. This is not a timing issue: resubmitting, waiting, or even deleting and recreating `src/reducers/<module>.ts` to force a fresh regenerate does not help — the file is recreated with the same stale body. Confirmed with a marker payload: the stored spec had it, the generated file didn't.

**Fixing or extending an already-scaffolded operation's reducer:** hand-edit `src/reducers/<module>.ts` directly — do not treat `src/` as generated-and-hands-off for this purpose. Whether that edit survives depends entirely on what happens next, and the two paths give opposite guarantees:

- **Local `ph generate` regeneration only (no further `docs mutate` against this document):** expected to be durable — everything you hand-edited (signature, parameter names, imports, comments, the reducer body) should survive. Unlike the clobber case below, this positive case has not itself been confirmed with a recorded test; treat it as the expected behavior, not an observed guarantee.
- **A subsequent `docs mutate` against this same document, for any reason — including the `setOperationReducer` resync recommended below:** codegen regenerates `src/reducers/<module>.ts` from the stored spec. Only the literal reducer **body** string tracked by the spec is guaranteed to reappear. Everything else you hand-edited in that file — a parameter rename (e.g. `action` → `_action` to satisfy a lint rule), added imports, comments — is silently overwritten back to whatever codegen derives from the spec, with no warning and no error. Confirmed: a `_action` rename was reverted by a same-body `setOperationReducer` call even though the reducer body itself was byte-identical.

So: also resubmit `setOperationReducer` with the same new reducer **body**, so the document model's stored specification stays in sync with the source for anyone reading the spec later — but do that resync *last*, after every other hand-edit to this file, since the resync call itself is a `docs mutate` and will re-clobber any non-body change made before it. Verify the fix by reading `src/reducers/<module>.ts` itself, not by reading back `docs get --state`, since the latter will look correct even when the former is untouched.

**A model id is burned once any operation has been added to it bare (without its reducer inline).** The freeze is tracked per **model id** (e.g. `acme-invoicing/pizza-order`), not per document instance, not per operation id — and it survives deleting the document entirely. A brand-new document created under the *same* model id inherits the old scaffolding, stub bodies and all, including operations from a document you already deleted. If hand-editing `src/` isn't a practical fix (e.g. you want a clean regenerate, or many operations are affected), the only real recovery is to abandon the model id and rebuild under a **new, never-before-used model id** in this reactor session, supplying every operation's reducer inline in its `addOperation` call from the very first one.

## Deletion and cleanup are not safe recovery tools

When abandoning a burned model id or a mistaken document, resist the urge to clean up by hand:

- `docs delete` does not remove the model from the package's generated barrel files (`document-models/document-models.ts`, `index.ts`, `upgrade-manifests.ts`). They keep importing from the deleted model's folder, and the next codegen pass — triggered by any unrelated mutation on a different document — silently re-adds the stale import.
- Manually deleting a model's generated folder from disk does **not** force a clean regenerate. The generator expects its own bookkeeping file there (e.g. `<model>.json`) and crashes on the next pass with a non-self-healing `ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '.../<model>.json'` that repeats on every subsequent mutation until something recreates that file.

Treat deletion as one-way and additive, not a correctable "undo": prefer leaving a dead model's folder and generated files in place over hand-removing them, and prefer a fresh model id over trying to reclaim a burned or deleted one. If an `ENOENT` loop like the above already happened, the only unblock (short of restarting the reactor) is to manually recreate an empty placeholder for the missing bookkeeping file so the generator's read succeeds again — an exception to "never write files under `document-models/` by hand", used only to break this specific stuck loop.

## Purity

Reducers are pure, synchronous functions. Forbidden inside a reducer:

- `crypto.randomUUID()`
- `new Date()`, `Date.now()`
- `Math.random()`
- external API calls, side effects, `async`/`await`, any other non-deterministic function

### Forbidden fallback patterns

```typescript
id: action.input.id || crypto.randomUUID();       // ❌ FORBIDDEN
timestamp: action.input.timestamp || new Date();  // ❌ FORBIDDEN
```

### Required pattern

Every dynamic value — ids for new entities, timestamps, anything system- or time-dependent — must arrive through `action.input`. Include the field in the operation's input schema (`id: OID!`, `timestamp: DateTime!`) and consume it as-is; never generate it inside the reducer. The caller dispatching the action is responsible for generating it beforehand.

## Complete example

A full module showing add, update (with optional fields), and delete:

```typescript
import type { MyModelItemsOperations } from "document-models/my-model/v1";

export const myModelItemsOperations: MyModelItemsOperations = {
  // ADD: all fields from input, compute derived values
  addItemOperation(state, action) {
    const amount = action.input.quantity * action.input.unitPrice;
    state.items.push({
      id: action.input.id,           // OID from input, never generated
      description: action.input.description,
      quantity: action.input.quantity,
      unitPrice: action.input.unitPrice,
      amount,                        // derived, not from input
    });
  },

  // UPDATE: optional input fields (InputMaybe<T>) map to non-optional state fields.
  // Use truthy checks — don't assign null to a non-nullable state property.
  updateItemOperation(state, action) {
    const item = state.items.find(i => i.id === action.input.id);
    if (!item) throw new ItemNotFoundError(`Item ${action.input.id} not found`);
    if (action.input.description) item.description = action.input.description;
    if (action.input.quantity) item.quantity = action.input.quantity;
    if (action.input.unitPrice) item.unitPrice = action.input.unitPrice;
    item.amount = item.quantity * item.unitPrice; // recalculate derived field
  },

  // DELETE: filter by id
  deleteItemOperation(state, action) {
    const index = state.items.findIndex(i => i.id === action.input.id);
    if (index === -1) throw new ItemNotFoundError(`Item ${action.input.id} not found`);
    state.items.splice(index, 1);
  },
};
```

Notes:
- Reducer functions take `(state, action)` — both are used in add/update/delete. If an operation truly doesn't need `action`, prefix it with an underscore (`_state`/`_action`) rather than dropping it.
- The `dispatch` parameter is optional and almost never needed — omit it.
- Mutate `state` directly; Mutative wraps the reducer.

## `Maybe` / `InputMaybe` handling

Optional input fields are typed `InputMaybe<T>` (`T | null | undefined`); optional state fields are typed `Maybe<T>` (`T | null`).

```typescript
// ❌ BAD — type error against Maybe<string>
amount: action.input.amount,
notes: action.input.notes,

// ✅ GOOD — matches Maybe<T> = T | null
amount: action.input.amount || null,
notes: action.input.notes || [],
```

Use truthy checks for conditional assignment, not `!== undefined`:

```typescript
// ❌ BAD — "Type 'string | null' is not assignable to type 'string'"
if (action.input.field !== undefined) entry.field = action.input.field;

// ✅ GOOD — truthy check
if (action.input.field) state.field = action.input.field;

// ✅ GOOD — booleans need an explicit null/undefined check instead of a truthy check
if (action.input.field !== undefined && action.input.field !== null)
  state.field = action.input.field;
```

## Errors

Define one named error per failure condition via `ADD_OPERATION_ERROR`:

- `code`: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, e.g. `"ENTRY_NOT_FOUND"`
- `name`: PascalCase ending in `Error`, e.g. `"EntryNotFoundError"`
- `description`: human-readable explanation of the error condition
- Names and ids must be unique across the document model

Throw by name. **The "don't import it yourself" rule below applies only to the reducer body string you submit inline via `addOperation`** — codegen auto-imports the error class into the generated file for you there, and adding your own import to that body string produces a duplicate import. It does **not** apply once you're hand-editing an already-generated `src/reducers/<module>.ts` file directly (per [03-implement-reducers.md](03-implement-reducers.md)): there the import is required and already present at the top of the file — do not delete it, and do add one yourself for any new error you introduce while hand-editing. Confirmed against a real hand-edited file: `document-models/pizza-order-desk/v1/src/reducers/basket.ts` imports its errors from `../../gen/basket/error.js` at the top, and that is correct there.

```typescript
// ✅ GOOD — inline addOperation reducer-body string: throw by name, auto-imported
if (entryIndex === -1) {
  throw new EntryNotFoundError(`Entry with ID ${action.input.id} not found`);
}

// ❌ BAD in either context — generic Error
throw new Error("Something went wrong");

// ❌ BAD in either context — nested error access
throw new errors.ModuleName.EntryNotFoundError("message");

// ❌ BAD only inside an inline addOperation reducer-body string — codegen already imports it there
import { EntryNotFoundError } from "../../gen/module-name/error.js";

// ✅ GOOD when hand-editing src/reducers/<module>.ts directly — this import is required here
import { EntryNotFoundError } from "../../gen/module-name/error.js";
```

Common error shapes: `EntityNotFoundError` (referenced entity doesn't exist), `DuplicateIdError` (id already exists on create), `InvalidInputError` (business logic violation), `PermissionDeniedError` (access control violation).

### How a thrown error actually surfaces — it does not propagate to the caller

A thrown named error does **not** escape `reducer()` as a JavaScript exception. The generated `reducer()` (built via `createReducer`) catches it internally and attaches its message to `operations.global[i].error` on the **document object that `reducer()` returns** — it does not re-throw, and it does not roll back state mutations made before the throw point in that same call. A test written as:

```typescript
// ❌ Never throws — reducer() catches the error and returns normally
expect(() => reducer(doc, confirmBooking({}))).toThrow("already confirmed");
```

will fail, because the call never throws. Assert on the returned document's operation error instead:

```typescript
// ✅ GOOD — check the operation's error field on the returned document
const updated = reducer(doc, confirmBooking({}));
const lastOp = updated.operations.global[updated.operations.global.length - 1];
expect(lastOp.error).toContain("already confirmed");
```

Don't assume the operation is otherwise a no-op when it errors: state changes made earlier in the same reducer call, before the throw, are not automatically rolled back — assert on the actual state fields too when a reducer can partially mutate state before an error condition is reached.
